title: The Bostrom Trilemma
description: Nick Bostrom's three-horned argument for taking simulation seriously

concepts.title: The Setup
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2003, philosopher Nick Bostrom published Are You Living in a Computer Simulation? in Philosophical Quarterly. The argument runs:

Assume that running ancestor-simulations is possible at sufficient technological maturity, and that some civilizations would want to run them. Then at least one of the following is true:

(1) Almost no civilizations reach the technological maturity required to run such simulations (they go extinct first).
(2) Civilizations that could run such simulations choose not to.
(3) We are almost certainly living in a simulation.

concepts.title: Why Three Horns?
concepts.contentHtml:
The structure is forced by counting. If even one mature civilization runs many ancestor-simulations, then simulated minds vastly outnumber 'base reality' minds.

If you're a typical mind — and you have no special reason to think otherwise — you should expect to be in the larger population: simulated.

So to escape conclusion (3), you must commit to either (1) — civilizations don't survive — or (2) — they survive but don't simulate.

concepts.title: Note: Not 'You ARE in a Sim'
concepts.contentHtml:
Bostrom does not argue that we're definitely simulated. He argues that at least one of (1), (2), or (3) must be true, and we don't currently have strong evidence ruling any out.

The argument is a constraint on possible futures, not a metaphysical claim. Even rejecting (3) requires accepting one of two strong claims about civilizations.

title: The Indifference Principle
description: Why the argument requires an assumption about typical observers

concepts.title: Self-Sampling Assumption
concepts.contentHtml:
Bostrom's argument relies on the Self-Sampling Assumption (SSA): you should reason as if you were a random sample from the set of observers in your reference class.

If 99% of observers like you are simulated, your prior credence that you are simulated should be ~99% — barring specific evidence pointing the other way.

This is the same logic that makes the Doomsday Argument work and underpins most anthropic reasoning.

concepts.title: Reference Class Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
SSA needs a reference class: which observers count as 'like you'? Humans? Conscious beings? Beings having subjective experience indistinguishable from yours?

The conclusion can flip depending on the choice. If 'like you' means 'consciousness on biological substrate', simulated digital minds don't count and the argument weakens. If it means 'any subjective experiencer indistinguishable from you', the population balance dominates.

Most critics of Bostrom's argument attack the reference class.

concepts.title: Substrate Independence
concepts.contentHtml:
A key premise: substrate independence — consciousness is computational, so it can run on silicon as well as on neurons.

If consciousness requires some specific biological feature (microtubules, particular electrochemistry), then no simulation can produce a conscious mind, and the argument collapses.

Substrate independence is widely held in philosophy of mind, but not universally. The argument's force depends on how much you accept it.

title: Computability Limits
description: Could a universe really be simulated by a computer inside it?

concepts.title: Coarse-Graining
concepts.contentHtml:
You don't need to simulate every quark to fool an inhabitant. You only need to simulate at the level the inhabitant can detect.

A modern video game renders detailed geometry only where the player looks. A simulation of human history could coarse-grain physics far below experimental sensitivity except where someone runs an experiment, then fill in detail on demand.

This drastically lowers the compute cost. Bostrom's estimates assume coarse-graining throughout.

concepts.title: The Bekenstein Bound
concepts.contentHtml:
Physical bounds limit computation. The Bekenstein bound caps the information content of a region by its surface area: roughly 10⁶⁹ bits per square meter at the holographic limit.

This means a simulating computer in a parent universe cannot simulate a universe larger or more detailed than itself in fundamental physics terms. Any simulation must be either smaller, simpler, or both.

So a simulated universe should expect to find resolution limits — and we do find them (Planck length, Heisenberg uncertainty, light-cone causality). Whether these are simulation artifacts or just physics is unresolved.

concepts.title: Glitches and Ancestor Simulations
concepts.contentHtml:
Could we detect a simulation? Proposed signatures: lattice artifacts in cosmic-ray spectra (Beane et al. 2012), subtle periodicities in physical constants, anomalies in long-distance entanglement.

None of these has produced a confirmed signal. Either we're not simulated, the simulators are too good to leave artifacts, or our detectors aren't sensitive enough.

Detection is in principle possible if the simulation uses discrete grids; impossible if it uses sufficiently sophisticated continuous interpolation.

title: Objections and Refinements
description: Where the argument might break and how it has been patched

concepts.title: The Recursion Objection
concepts.contentHtml:
If simulated civilizations can themselves run simulations, the population of simulated minds explodes recursively. But each layer must be smaller (Bekenstein bound), so the recursion must terminate.

If recursion is shallow (one or two layers), the typical observer is in an upper layer. If it's deep (many layers), the typical observer is near the bottom — and resolution there should be visibly degraded.

Tegmark and others use this to argue we're either not simulated or in a high-fidelity outer layer.

concepts.title: The Motivation Objection
concepts.contentHtml:
Why would a mature civilization simulate ancestors? Possible reasons: research, entertainment, ethical obligation to instantiate experiences worth having. Possible reasons against: simulating suffering is morally unacceptable; compute can be better spent.

This is the horn about which we know least. Conclusion (2) — that mature civilizations don't simulate — could be true purely on ethical grounds. Some philosophers find this the most likely escape.

concepts.title: Why It Doesn't Matter (Maybe)
concepts.contentHtml:
Even if you accept conclusion (3), what changes? You still feel pain, love, hunger. The laws of physics still constrain your actions. Other people are still real to you.

David Chalmers argues that simulation is a metaphysical hypothesis like idealism: it changes what reality fundamentally is, but doesn't change anything experientially. The chair is still solid; it's just made of computation rather than atoms.

Pragmatically, life inside a simulation is the only life we have, and the same rules of caring, knowing, and acting apply.

title: Related Hypotheses
description: Boltzmann brains, dust theory, and the broader landscape

concepts.title: Boltzmann Brains
concepts.contentHtml:
In an infinite or extremely long-lived universe, statistical fluctuations could spontaneously assemble a brain with all your memories, complete with the impression of a coherent past — a Boltzmann brain.

If such fluctuations are common enough, they might outnumber 'real' observers. You should then doubt your memories.

Cosmologists treat this as a serious problem: any cosmological model that predicts more Boltzmann brains than ordinary observers is considered a strike against that model. Sean Carroll calls it 'cognitive instability'.

concepts.title: Dust Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Greg Egan's Permutation City proposes dust theory: any sufficiently complex system contains, by random correspondence, the computation of any other system. Therefore, every conscious experience is being implemented somewhere by random matter, all the time.

If true, simulation isn't a special claim — it's the default. Every possible mind exists in every cubic meter of dust.

Most philosophers reject this on grounds that 'computation' requires more than mere correspondence — it requires causal structure. But the argument has bite.

concepts.title: The Mathematical Universe
concepts.contentHtml:
Max Tegmark's Mathematical Universe Hypothesis goes further: every mathematically consistent structure exists physically. Our universe is just one such structure.

Under MUH, simulation reduces to: 'is our universe being computed by another universe?' But every consistent computation already exists mathematically, so the distinction between 'real' and 'simulated' may be empty.

This is metaphysically extreme but takes anthropic reasoning to its logical conclusion: if existence is just consistency, then everything that can exist, does — and you find yourself in one of the consistent options.
